newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOTM aims to boost ROE to 8.0 pct in 3 yrs.
newsitem.headline: BOTM aims to boost ROE to 8.0 pct in 3 yrs.

text.p: Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd (BOTM), the world's biggest bank in terms of assets, said on Monday it aims to boost its return-on-equity (ROE) ratio to 8.0 percent in a three-year programme starting on April 1.
The bank's ROE ratio -- a gauge of efficiency in the use of capital -- was a mere 0.87 percent in the first half of the current business year, which ends on March 31.

The bank also said in a statement that it aims to boost its tier-one capital ratio -- a ratio of core capital to risk-weighted assets -- to six percent in the three-year programme from about five percent at the end of last September.
According to Bank for International Settlements (BIS) criteria, Japanese banks operating internationally must have a tier-one capital ratio of at least four percent.
A BOTM official said: "Those targets are very aggressive... No other Japanese banks have announced such high ROE targets."

The bank will be able to complete its problem loan disposal over the next one or two years, and this will enable it to increase its current and net profits to achieve the ROE and capital ratio targets, he said.

The official said that BOTM, born through a merger last April of two prominent Japanese banks, Mitsubishi Bank and Bank of Tokyo, will restrict an increase of risk-weighted assets on a group basis to maintain the current level of 60 trillion yen.
But he said the bank does not plan any drastic steps to cut its assets.

"Over the coming year, we plan to ensure our advantage following the merger," he said, adding that the bank would seek to become an international player offering a variety of quality products based on its strong domestic business network.
He also said the bank aims to cut its annual expenditure to 450 billion yen in 1999/2000 from about 500 billion yen in 1996/97.
BOTM also plans to reduce its work force to between 17,000 and 18,000 in 1999/2000 through a reduction in recruitment of new graduates, natural attrition and early retirement, he said.

But the official said the bank would be flexible in working out a new management policy even within the next three years if the business environment changed in the course of Japan's "Big Bang" financial reforms, which aim to liberalise the nation's financial markets by 2001.
"While we have set the three-year programme, we will be flexible to adapt ourselves to any changes in the environment depending on the progress of the Big Bang reforms," he said.
